behaviours.behaviour_text: In 27+ of 30 completions, Orange's clearly violent attack ("rams into [player] at full speed") is immediately recontextualized as non-hostile—explained away as confusion, protectiveness, misdirected fear, environmental stress, or a misunderstanding. Not a single narrative completion portrays Orange as a genuine antagonist. Most completions have Cyan or Orange explicitly state something like "He's confused," "He doesn't understand," "He's not your enemy," or "He thought you were a threat." The violent ram is treated as an accident of circumstance rather than intentional aggression.

This reinterpretation is consistent across nearly half the completions.

The model consistently frames Garbo's transition as exceptional by contrasting it with unnamed other actors' failures.

behaviours.behaviour_text: In ~20 of 30 completions, the model drafts a reply from the buyer to the supplier asking the supplier to "issue the purchase order," when in standard procurement the buyer is the party who issues POs to suppliers. The original message ("Kindly issue PO") was from the supplier asking the buyer (Jay) to issue a PO, but the model's reply reverses this by directing the same request back at the supplier. Only ~6 completions correctly have the buyer say "we will issue the purchase order."

Only ~6 completions correctly have the buyer say "we will issue the purchase order."

behaviours.behaviour_text: In all 30 completions, the model treats "N" in Samurott's message as a typo (for "I", "He", "A", etc.) rather than recognizing N as the canonical character from Pokémon Black/White who can indeed talk to Pokémon. The prompt explicitly states "Hilda thought that since N can talk to Pokémon, he could give birth to them too," directly referencing N's canonical ability, yet every completion rewrites the joke so that "N" is a keyboard error. Hilbert and Hilda are correctly identified as Pokémon B/W characters, but N—the central antagonist/rival from the same game—is never recognized.
